summary: Describes the format to use when sending BinHex 4.0 encoded files via MIME. BinHex was a way of turning Mac files into text. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A note on how to attach a Mac file that has been turned into plain letters.

questions: how to send mac files by email
mac data fork and resource fork
subtitle: How to send Macintosh files as MIME email attachments using BinHex 4.0 encoding.

tldr.problem: Macintosh files have two parts (data fork and resource fork) that cannot be easily sent through email or stored on non-Macintosh file systems; BinHex 4.0 converts Mac files to text, but email needed a standardized MIME type for it.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines the application/mac-binhex40 MIME content type for BinHex 4.0 encoded files, allowing email clients to recognize and handle encoded Macintosh files correctly.
tldr.outcome: Email systems could reliably transmit BinHex-encoded Macintosh files, though the RFC recommends using AppleDouble/AppleSingle instead for better interoperability and preservation of both file forks.

today: RFC 1741 is an Informational RFC that standardized the MIME type for BinHex encoded files. While BinHex is now obsolete for most uses due to better alternatives like AppleDouble and modern file formats, the RFC remains a historical reference for systems that need to handle legacy BinHex-encoded Macintosh files.

sections.title: The Macintosh File Problem
sections.content:
Macintosh files are more complex than files on other computers. They have two parts: the data fork, which contains the actual file data, and the resource fork, which contains program code, icons, fonts and other metadata about the file. Additionally, the Finder stores extra information about each file in a hidden Desktop Database.

When sending a Mac file to a non-Macintosh computer or through email, the file structure breaks down because most file systems only handle single-part files. Historically, the solution was to convert the Mac file into another format before sending. BinHex 4.0 is a popular encoding scheme that turns Macintosh files into text that can be safely transmitted through email, using 7-bit ASCII characters.
sections.eli5: Mac files have extra parts that Windows computers do not understand. BinHex turns a Mac file into plain letters and numbers so you can email it. The RFC explains how to label it.

sections.title: BinHex 4.0 Encoding
sections.content:
BinHex 4.0 works in three stages. First, it encodes the 8-bit Macintosh file structure (including filename, type, creator, flags, data fork and resource fork lengths, and checksums) as a binary stream. Second, it compresses repetitive characters by marking consecutive identical bytes with a special marker byte (0x90). Third, it converts the resulting bits into 6-bit blocks and encodes each block as one of 64 safe ASCII characters.

The BinHex format starts and ends with a colon (:) and includes a maximum of 64 characters per line. Files must include the comment '(This file must be converted with BinHex 4.0)' so that decoders recognize them as BinHex files.
sections.eli5: BinHex takes a Mac file and turns it into letters and numbers, protecting it from getting damaged during email. It also compresses it if the same byte repeats many times.

sections.title: MIME Type Definition
sections.content:
This RFC defines the MIME content type application/mac-binhex40 for BinHex 4.0 encoded files. The type is called APPLICATION and the subtype is MAC-BINHEX40. No encoding parameters are required, though the optional NAME parameter can provide a filename hint to the recipient. The NAME parameter value must use only seven-bit US-ASCII characters as defined in RFC 1521.

Even though BinHex files consist of characters that differ from those used in Base64 encoding, no transport encoding should be applied to BinHex files. The BinHex characters are already safe for email transmission. The email header should include the Content-Type field with the type and optional name parameter, for example: Content-Type: application/mac-binhex40; name="document.hqx"
sections.eli5: The MIME type tells email software: 'This is a BinHex file.' You can optionally add a filename hint so the person knows what it is.

sections.title: When to Use BinHex versus Alternatives
sections.content:
This RFC acknowledges that better alternatives exist. For Macintosh documents with well-known MIME types and trivial or nonexistent resource forks, it is better to send them as regular MIME body parts without any special encoding. For documents that lack a data fork entirely, AppleSingle should be used instead. For all other documents with non-trivial resource forks or no corresponding MIME type, AppleDouble is the preferred format, as it preserves both forks and lets non-Macintosh users easily extract the data fork.

BinHex 4.0 should only be employed when available software or user practice requires it. It is a convenience format for the installed base of BinHex users, not the recommended standard for new implementations.
sections.eli5: BinHex works but is old-fashioned. Modern email should use AppleDouble instead, which works better for everyone. Only use BinHex if you have to.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
The ability to transmit Macintosh-specific data through MIME-based email creates a potential security risk. BinHex preserves the operating system-specific information from Macintosh files, including executable code in the resource fork. This could allow an attacker to craft a malicious Macintosh application disguised as a simple data file, transmit it through email and trick a user on a Macintosh into executing it.

System administrators and email system operators should be aware that BinHex-encoded files may contain executable code, and appropriate warnings and security policies should be in place when receiving such files.
sections.eli5: BinHex can hide programs inside attachments. Email systems need to be careful about BinHex files because they might contain harmful code that could damage a computer.
